The purpose of requiring a distinction in the affidavit is really as far as possible to secure that men who are qualified in a particular district shall vote there, and to avoid a possible consequence of depleting some one or more electoral districts, and perhaps overloading the electoral districts in which the men have been just before they enlisted. I see no particular objection to substituting the word " entitled," as suggested by my hon. friend, for the word " qualified," but it seems to me it will amount to practically the same thing. A man who swears that he is entitled to something has to determine a question of legal right on his part, just as much as if he has to swear he is qualified. Both expressions are open to the objection that analysing them strictly they imply not only a statement of fact but of judgment by the person making the statement of fact, that that fact, by law, qualifies him or entitles him to a certain thing. I think there is no great risk involved in using in these affidavits with regard to our soldiers the words which are used in other affidavits with regard to people generally. I think experience goes to show that those who are called upon to take oaths of this kind realize that what they are swearing to is as to the existence of a particular fact upon which, as they understand it, their qualification rests.

While I am quite willing to accept the explanation of the minister with regard to the age limit, I am not willing to accept the reasons he gave. The Minister of Justice has said that because a

young man in civilian life is not entitled to a vote until he becomes twenty-one years of age, therefore he should not be entitled to a vote in soldier life until he reaches that age. That is entirely contrary to the spirit on which the Bill is founded, which is, that the young man who is serving his country is entitled to special consideration in regard to the exercise of his franchise. That being so, the young man who by reason of his being of an age sufficient to give -the full service to his country that he would if he were twenty-one years or over, is surely entitled to the same advantage of franchise as if he were twenty-one years or older. The civilian qualification is based upon certain well set out conditions, the young civilian on attaining the age of twenty-one being liable to certain legal conditions. There is a change in his status between 20 and 22, which makes the difference between the civilian voter and the civilian non-voter by reason of age; but there is no such difference in status between the boy of eighteen and the young man of twenty-two in regard to his military service. I merely wish to draw attention to this fact; I am not wishing to make legislation for the Government or for the minister; but while I am willing to let the matter go as he has explained it, I do not wish to be understood as agreeing to the reasons he gave.
In regard to the residence qualification, I took exception to this proviso when the Bill came to the House first; and, after all has been said, I still maintain that this proviso is unnecessarily confusing in the proper exercise of the right of the voter. It is quite true that if the voter has a right to vote in a certain district, he can cast his vote in that district; but when you come to make a distinction between the man who has a right to vote in a district and the man who has not a right to vote in a district, you practically give an opportunity of switching ballots, which is something that is not desirable, I am sure, from the point of view of the minister. We must do the best we can under the circumstances we have to meet; and my contention is that we shall have a law that will give to the soldier the right to cast his ballot if we strike out this proviso, and by striking it out we shall be much more certain that the ballot will be cast in one case as it is in the other; that is, that there will be a similarity of treatment and action of the soldiers in the direction of where their ballots will go. I do not wish to introduce

personal matters into this discussion, but let me do it merely in order to illustrate my point. There are in training now in Edmonton and its immediate vicinity two regiments of infantry and a squadron of cavalry, the men having been recruited from the country surrounding Edmonton. Owing to the delay in enlistments for the second and third contingents many of these men were residents of either East Edmonton or West Edmonton for thirty days before they enlisted.
I am speaking now of tne constituency of West Edmonton, for which I have received the Liberal nomination. The soldiers may have had the right to vote in other districts, or they may not have had that right; but when their votes come to be cast, there is a very great possibility in one constituency of the votes being massed to he cast in that constituency, and in the other constituency of the votes being distributed over the localities from which the men came. This is not a sound principle; it is neither necessary nor right. As I have said, I do not wish to make this matter personal; but the candidate nominated by the Conservative party in the constituency of West Edmonton is the senior colonel of the two regiments to which I have referred, so that the matter is entirely under his control. I do not wish to make any suggestion against this gentleman, that he is likely to take particular advantage of his situation but I am saying that that is the situation, and not only do I think I am doing what is right when I bring the concrete facts before the House, but I think the minister will be 4 p.m. wise to consider the situation in the light of the facts I have stated to him. The political conditions in this Bill go pretty close home to the city of Edmonton, and that is why I am venturing to take up the time of the House and the minister in discussing this Bill.

I am not sure whether I have understood the hon. member sufficiently clearly to reply to him, but I do not see how the ambiguity arises that he fears. A man on the list who has a right to vote in any constituency has no option thereafter. He is bound to exercise that right.

There are no listis in
Alberta.

There are no lists now. Lists, of course, are to be made up. Do I understand the hon. gentleman's remarks to apply to certain districts in which there is the right to swear in on election day?
148i

In those provinces where there are no standard lists, there is no way of checking beforehand the status of the voter; it is all a matter of enumeration immediately before the election, and therefore there is not the same possibility of verifying any condition in regard to any voter, on the part of himself or on the part of any one else, that there is in other parts of the country. Apart from that, the condition is the same in all parts of the country.

If I understand the hon. gentleman aright, he says that the right in Alberta and Saskatchewan of a man to swear in if his name is absent from the list, taken in conjunction with this Bill, leaves that voter, if he is a volunteer, in a position practically to elect where his vote shall go.
Yes.

The minister is more able to deal with such details than I am; but it appears that in so far as this Bill may not provide certainty it is incidental to the system of list-making in Alberta and Saskatchewan.
What I arose chiefly to do was to put before the bommittee my own view as to the question raised by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) and repeated by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), as to the extension of the franchise to all soldiers although they may not have reached their majority. I take the view that the Bill in that respect is right. I do not look on the extension of the franchise to the soldiers as in any way a quid pro quo, as in any way a benignant action on the part of the state to him in virtue of his soldiership. It appears to me that in regard to the British franchise the law presumes, that if the individual man has a real patriotic interest in his country's affairs, and secondly, if he is competent to express that interest, that man is entitled to vote. We take certain precautions to ascertain whether he lives up to these two requirements-whether he has a real patriotic interest in his country's affairs and whether he is competent to express that interest. We say that he must be a resident, that he must live so long in a certain locality. If he is a rolling stone, we cannot presume that he has that fixed and determined interest that he otherwise will have. On the other hand, in order to ascertain whether he is competent to express his vote or not, we fix the age of twenty-one as the age of maturity at

which he arrives at competency. Then we say that a judge by virtue of the restraints of his office is incompetent to express his interest. Then we come here and make an extension of the franchise in one respect; that is, we do not insist upon the condition of fixed residence. To that extent and no more, there is in this Bill an extension of the franchise.
Why do we make that extension? Have we a right ito presume that real interest in the affairs of this country which ordinarily is considered proved by fixity of residence? I think we have. The very fact of his enlistment, even though being a British subject he comes from the United States, and has not fulfilled the requirement of three months' residence in the locality or a year's residence in the province, gives us the right to presume that he has a patriotic interest in the affairs of Canada. Consequently, we do away with ' the old requirement.
But the hon. member for Bonaventure says we ought to do more; that we ought to presume that he is competent to express his interest even though under age because he has enlisted.

Provided he is at least
18 years of age.

Provided he is 18. I
do not see that the fact that he enlists should in any way convince Parliament that he has reached a higher degree of mental maturity than other men. His enlistment undoubtedly is an expression of a loyal interest in the affairs of the country, but it is an expression of loyal interest only; it is not proof that he has a'greater mental development than his fellows. 1 think - the right hon. leader of the Opposition is wrong when he says that we should bann this measure because it extends the franchise. It extends the franchise only in a direction where we have a right to presume the requirement fulfilled which otherwise we demand of the voter, namely, an interest in his country's affairs. T think the hon. member for Bonaventure is wrong when he complains not that we are extending the franchise, but that we are not extending it far enough, because The direction in which he wishes it extended is a direction as to which no pre-*sumption by virtue of enlistment arises at all.

Never since
1897 have we undertaken to define the franchise. That has been left entirely to "the provinces, and in view of the fact that
[Mr. Meighen.J
you are extending the franchise to those who go to fight, you are not in a position to answer the contention of the hon. member for Bonaventure. The Government are determined that they will not alter the qualification of voters with respect to age. But what I rose particularly to deal with is a statement which I have just heard on the the part of my hon. friend, namely, that lists will be made. This is the first intimation we have received that lists are to be made in connection with the voting of the soldiers.
I did not say that.; I do not know what sentence my hon. friend refers to.
I had said that there were no lists in Alberta.
I understood that the hon. gentleman said that lists are to be made.
Lists must be made in Alberta and Saskatchewan under the present Act.
There are no lists in Alberta and Saskatchewan.
But they are made by enumerators prior to the election.

Exactly. If no lists are to be sent to the front, matters will be further complicated, and that is why I want to inquire as to whether or not lists are to be made. If the lists made in Alberta and Saskatchewan are not to be sent to the front, how will the soldier be able to establish that he is qualified to vote? This only goes to show how many difficulties there are in this proposed legislation. Parliament has decided in favour of the Bill; therefore I shall not press any objection as to the principle of it; but my hon. friend the Minister of Justice has invited suggestions, and I may tell him that I am prepared to offer an amendment. The great objection to this Bill is that it puts aside altogether the safeguards which we have considered to be necessary in connection with elections in this country. If we have an election-and the hon. Minister of Public Works this morning, during the course of his speech, gave us due warning that we are going to have an election- every vote that is cast in Canada will be surrounded with all the safeguards that it is possible to provide. Yesterday I was struck with the speech of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett), who told us that

notwithstanding all the precautions with which the law has endeavoured to surround the sacred rights of the franchise, fraud after fraud has been committed. At election -time, party spirit runs very high. I stated the other day-and I do not believe that any hon. gentleman will question my statement-that during the course of an election offences are committed against the law, actuated by party spirit, which would not be committed by a man in connection with his private affairs. Am I wrong in this? Is any one prepared to say that I am not right? It is the experience of every man in this committee that during elections the law has been violated by most respectable citizens, who did for their party what they would not have done for themselves. It is said by hon. gentlemen opposite that the men who go to the front and who are ready to shed their blood for their country will not do anything wrong in this respect. I have the greatest possible confidence in the men who have gone' to the front; but, after all, they are but flesh and blood, and are subject to the same temptations to which other men are subjected. Every day, in the prayer which is said in this House, we say, " Lead us not into temptation;" yet it is proposed to put temptation in the way of these men, and to trust that everything will be done correctly. I ask fairly and with all sincerity, is that business? Is that proper legislation? Should not at least more precautions be taken in order to ensure that this method of voting shall be carried out with some degree of honesty and faithfulness? I have a good many friends at the front; hon. gentlemen opposite also have many friends at the front. I have great confidence in them, but I am not prepared to say that there shall not be some delinquency; I have yet to learn of any human activity in connection with which, at some time or upon some occasion, there has not been delinquency. All I ask is that more precautions be provided in connection with this proposed legislation. If it is not possible to take some of the precautions adopted in connection with elections at home, give us some precautions which will ensure that the franchise shall be exercised with the same degree of fidelity and faithfulness as we expect it to be exercised in connection with the voting in this country. As the Bill is now drafted my hon. friend cannot tell me who will be the officers who will take the oath and do the recording.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I concede that under the Bill as drafted I could not tell that. I have
made more precise the disposition to deal with that.
Very good; he has made the language more precise. Has the amendment been printed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, it has not been possible to have the amendment printed.

My hon. friend has probably made an amendment to his draft to say that either the colonel, or the major, or the captain, or the lieutenant is to take the vote. But whoever takes the votes takes them without any check upon him. Would my hon. friend the Minister of Justice think of having the votes which are going do be recorded in Canada by the-returning officers cast without any check, upon the returning officers, without administering any oath to them and without having any scrutineers over them, with no protection to assure that the vote of the electors would he properly recorded? He would not think of doing so. If it were attempted every one would say it was an outrage. No Government has ever done it. Now, the limit of my hon. friend's amendment to the present draft is that he will delegate somebody in the army to take the vote. Since the vote has to be taken as a vote for the Government or for the Opposition, a disposition which I do not like but to which we have to submit, will my hon. friend agree to a commission of two, appointed by the Government to represent both the Government and the Opposition, to go to the front and take the vote? Then these commissioners will check one another and will ensure that the vote is honestly taken. That is not an extraordinary precaution. The vote in Canada we can deal with later; we are most concerned with the vote to he taken in Europe, because there are more o-f our soldiers there. I suggest to my hon. friend that he would singularly improve this Bill if he were to provide that the vote shall be taken by two commissioners appointed under it to represent both the Government and the Opposition, and to ensure, after all, some degree of absolute faithfulness in the discharge of these duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Before I answer the suggestion I would like to say one word with reference to some observations of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). I do not propose to repeat anything I have said with regard to the age qualification But the hon. gentleman expressed what I might call his apprehension that in the par-

ticular case in which he is especially interested the colonel might be an undesirable element, from his point of view, if he had any control of these votes. The proposal I intend to make with regard to the method of the ballot reaching the soldiers and the vote being taken would pass quite by the colonel, leave him quite on the outside, so that in that especial respect my hon. friend has nothing to fear. What we propose to suggest is to utilize the machinery whereby these men are paid and have these ballots given to them through the paymasters. The paymasters are not combatant officers. I have ascertained from the Paymaster General here that there exists a system by which these ballots could pass to the paymaster in England, and from there the assistant paymasters and the regimental paymasters would bring them to each smaller unit, that is the squadron or the company or the battery. They bring the men their money, and suTely they could bring the ballots to them.' These ballots would in that way reach the officers commanding the companies or squadrons or batteries, according to the nature of the force. With regard to the suggestion the right hon. gentleman has made, of course I would not do otherwise than consider any suggestion the right hon. gentleman would make. The first objection to the suggestion that occurs to me at the moment is that I doubt its practicability. We have to remember that we have to reach a large number of men, 30,000 ot 40,000 or 50,000, scattered over a considerable territory; and for any two men to gather all the votes of these men, I am afraid would take a very long period of time, longer I may say than the interval that would elapse-
Ordinarily there is 30 days between the issue of -the writ and the voting.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Let us take 30 days. We have to bear in mind that these ballots have to get from London to the men, and -that after the vote has been taken they have to get back -here to Canada -again, and I would be afraid it would not be practicable to have that looked after by two men. If the idea could be put into practice it would be necessary that we should have a number of couples of -men who could divide the work -between them. That might work out in a more practical way. If they aTe to go two, whose report is to prevail? Supposing they go two, and as they started out in disagreement I sup-

pose that we -have some reason to expect that they would return in disagreement, whose report would be final? I do not know whether it is intended simply that they should bring back the ballots or that they should make -a -report. I would have great fear that we -would not get any agreement between the members of -such a commission.
What would they differ about?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not just grasp what it is they are to report.

They would put the certificate on the envelope -and send it to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery.
Mr. DOHERTY; Might I suggest that we should consider this when we come to the section dealing with the method in which the votes a-re to be taken?
Yes. I threw it out in advance so that we might take it up when we reached that section.

Reverting to section 1, this is a matter on which each has his own personal view. A good deal of our difib culty would have been obvi-a-ted as to the qualification, if the Government o-r the committee had adopted the principle that the going to the front of the soldier should not deprive him of -any right which he -had before he went. That would leave the qualification the same, and would get rid of a great deal of difference of opinion as to what that qualification ought to be; and it would not open up the question of an enlargement of the franchise. I am strongly of the opinion that 21 is the proper age. I admit that if you change the age to something else, you can keep on changing it by the same argument. I h ve not heard any good reason advanced why we should change from the age limit that we have always had. After mature deliberation it has been decided in this country that a man has not reached the proper years of maturity at which he is able to vote until he is 21. I do not think the fact of his going to the front changes the principle at all, for a man of 21 years of age is the same at the front as he is at home, loyal and brave and patriotic though he may be. I think we should get rid of a lot of the difficulty if we took the ground, which several speakers on the Government side of the House as well as speakers on this side have taken, that the men who have gone to fight for their country should

not be deprived of the rights of citizenship which they had before they went. .

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I recognize that there
is force in that. But this consideration was impressed upon the minds of the committee:	that a large number of men
who, when they left home, were not qualified voters would, if they had stayed at home, have been in a position to complete what was required to enable them to get a vote. For instance, I understand that in the large cities of Ontario at all events, there is, after the election has been called, a registration which brings in a large number of people, and they get their votes. Now every soldier who would have been in a position to avail himself of that opportunity is deprived of it because he is away; and this applies not only to Ontario, but to the western provinces, where enumerators are appointed to make out lists after an election has been called. Now there will be many soldiers who if they had stayed at home would have been enumerated and got their votes-that is those who had the proper qualifications-and even if they were not enumerated they could get their votes simply by walking in to the poll and swearing to their qualifications. I think it is generally recognized as being true that we have a large proportion of recruits from those western provinces, and that the cities in the East have contributed at all events a highly creditable proportion; and if we are correct in our assumption that many of these would have got their votes but for their absence on military affairs, we reduce to a comparatively small number those who would not have got the vote if they had been at home, and are now getting it because of being -soldiers. For myself, I am glad to see them get votes, but if there be objection with regard to that, there is this to be said in support of it. The hon. gentleman says that it would simplify things to let only those vote who were qualified to vote; but it seems to me that if you are willing to take in the mam whose absence of qualifications results solely from his absence from the country, it is not worth while, in view of the presumably small number left, to create the necessity of distinguishing betweeen your soldiers. In this Bill we get a distinction as between tho-se who aTe over and those who are under 21, but we are adhering to the view that a. m-an is a man when he is 21. We certainly should not be able to find out who were the men who, not having qualified at the time they enlisted, could have got themselves registered if they had been at home; and if we said that only those should vote who are now qualified we should be excluding not only those who if they had been at home would not have got a vote, but also a large number of those who if they had been at home could have got a vote. The simplification of the thing was one consideration that weighed with us, and we came to the conclusion that not only the proper way but the simplest way was to give every soldier a vote.

I do not wish to prolong the discussion, but I wish to make clear that I am in favour of giving every man a vote who would have had the right to a vote had he remained at home. I meant to cover that class of men.
M-r. DOHERTY:	We could not -ascertain th-at.

This Bill is to give soldiers who are away from home an opportunity to vote if an election takes place during the w.ar. That election may or may not take place during the war, and I should like to ask the minister whether he has ever considered the advisability of looking after the suffrage of the soldier after he -returns from the war. A great many of these soldiers will not be on the voters lists when they return. They will not be entitled to vote as soldiers, and I think a great many of them will be disfranchised.
I think that we should be just as solicitous in looking after the suffrage of the soldier after he returns from the war as when he is at the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I may say that the question that was referred to the committee was: What could we do in the way of giving votes to soldiers who were out of the country or away from home? and I have to admit that we did not get beyond the question that was referred to us: and perhaps some things that have been seen and heard would indicate that we did not need to look for further difficulties, but that quite a few presented themselves within the bounds of the question referred to us. I quite recognize that the situation that my hon. friend has spoken of is one that will call for action, if that is possible, before we are confronted with it, but I am afraid I can hardly undertake to deal with it just now.

I think that there need be no apprehension so far as Ontario is concerned. Looking over the statutes I

find that I was wrong. The statute has been amended since my time, so that those absent on militia service can be retained on the list. If I could show that my son or brother was absent on militia service, his name would be retained on the list.
What if he was not on the list?
That would not make any difference; he could be put on the list.
He has to appear in court and prove that he is 21 years of age and a British subject.

Not under the law of Ontario. If he is abser<+ on militia duty, or through his duties as a fisherman or lumberman, his father can put him on the list. That covers the unmarried man. As to the married man, his residence does not change so long as his family continues to live at the same place; so he would be kept on the list, or if he was not on the list he could be put on. I think the point raised by the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Hugh Clark) is covered by the Ontario statutes at the present time. I did not think that was the case the other night when I spoke.
I understand there have been some amendments to clause 1. Will you, Mr. Chairman, please read them?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is proposed to substitute a redraft for section 1. We strike out the words "or enrolled" in fixing the period of time for residence anterior to date of enlistment or enrolment. It was pointed out that the word "enrolled" added nothing to the word "enlisted." The second change is intended to make clear that the thirty days' residence in a place required to give qualification under this section must be within the last six months preceding the enlistment. In view of the possibility that a man might have resided in more than one place for a period of thirty days within the last six months preceding his enlistment, it is provided that the place in which he shall be qualified shall be the place at which he last resided for thirty days during that last day six months.
Suppose he only resided two or three days where he was enlisted?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If he only resided two or three days where he was enlisted he will not get a vote from there but, if there is any other place within an electoral district in Canada in which he has, within six months previous to his enlistment, had a 
residence for thirty days, he can qualifiy in that electoral district. Some one pointed out the other day that it might happen that a man, having lived thirty days, or perhaps a year, in a particular constituency, might, for the purpose of enlistment, go down to some other place and be there three or four days before enlisting. He could not say that for thirty days immediately preceding his enlistment he had been in the original place and as he had not been thirty days in the place where he was enlisted he could not qualify there.

We are not talking about residence; we are talking about a legal term. There has been many a case threshed out in the courts of Canada as to what constitutes residence. The condition in my own province is very much the same as it is in the province of Quebec. We have a list prepared once a year and when that list is closed there is no possibility of getting another name added to it. Any man who has resided in the province of New Brunswick for six months prior to the 24th day of August is entitled to have his name placed on the list in the district in which he then resides. Take a young man who has no home or take, for instance, an immigrant. He has lived, we will say, in the county of Carleton for a few weeks or months-no home, no wife, no friends; he has worked somewhere for a few weeks; he has moved from there to the county of York; perhaps he has worked in the shanty for a few weeks; he has moved from there to St. John; he has happened to be there, for five weeks and he has enlisted at St. John-as I understand this provision, it would give him the right to elect that Sit. John would be his residence.
-Mr. DOHERTY: Yes.

The difficulty is that that man, under the law of New Brunswick, would not have a right at all to be on the voters' list on the score of residence, not having had a fixed residence for six months prior to the 24th of August.

Although he would not otherwise have the right, the very fact of his enlistment would justify us in giving him that right, would it not?
Mr . CARVELL: That is the whole question that we have been discussing here. I am now discussing this first clause, and I am pointing out the difficulty of knowing where this man's vote would be cast. In my opinion this only makes it easier to have

these votes distributed where they are most needed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is quite true that we are giving the vote to a man for a thirty days' residence. We have never pretended to give the vote only to a man who would be qualified under the provincial franchise. What we have endeavoured to do is prevent him from making a choice of the place he shall give as the place of his thirty days' residence. We get at the proof of the thirty days' qualification in the same way as it would be got at under the provincial franchise, and if a man is truthful in his affidavit, we tie him down to the last place in which he has resided for thirty days.

This Government ought
to do one thing or the other. They should either simply give the right to soldiers to vote at the election provided they would have the right to vote if they had been at home. That would be in accordance with the argument which has been made by gentlemen who support the Bill and who say that it would be a great hardship to deprive a man of his right to vote simply because he happens to be abroad in the service of his country. But you confer the right to vote upon soldiers who, if at home, could not have a vote and you are including a class of people to whom you give a greater right than would have been given to them if they had remained at home. I think you should either limit this right to those who, if at home, would have the right to vote or extend it to all soldiers who are engaged in the Canadian forces, no matter whether they are under 21 years or not. That is the logical position to take. The Minister of Justice admits that he is giving a new franchise to the soldiers. He is giving those the right to vote who, under the present electoral law, would not have the right to vote in many cases if they were at home. He is allowing soldiers who have not been residents of Canada at all, who may simply be temporarily in the country, who may have come from the West Indies, or the United States, or other countries, to serve under the British flag and who have found it convenient to enlist in the Canadian army, the right to vote simply on the ground that they have been in Canada for a period of thirty days. He justifies that on the ground that men who are willing to go to the front and risk their lives in defence of the country should be recognized by giving them right of citizenship. After all, the privilege of casting the ballot is the highest expression
in the law of the right of citizenship. This Bill proposes to give the right of citizenship to many soldiers because they have gone to the front and risked their lives for the defence of the country. If that is the principle upon which the minister is proceeding, why not give that same right of citizenship to all who are deemed by the Government to be capable of bearing arms, worthy to be sent to the front and worthy to take their share in the defence of the Empire? The Solicitor General says that the age of 21 is looked upon as the age of maturity. How absurd it is to say that it shall be deemed the age of maturity as to the casting of a ballot, and that it shall not be deemed the age of maturity in respect to the soldier who goes into training, goes to the front and is thought to have sufficient judgment to make a good soldier. It requires good mentality for a man to become a good soldier, and the law deems a man over 18 years of age fit to be a good soldier and to fight for his country. Why not give to the young man who has lived all his life in Canada this highest right of citizenship, if you are going to give it to a soldier who has been only within our gates for a few days, and who may know nothing about the issues which divide the people, and to whom in many cases it would be a matter of supreme indifference whether he cast his vote for the Government or for the Opposition.

The hon. gentleman
characterized my statement as absurd when I said that the age of maturity for the purposes of exercising all the functions of citizenship might well remain at Itwenty-one years, and that that was not inconsistent with permitting a citizen at eighteen years of age to enlist to take his part in the war. In thus disagreeing with me, I do not think that the hon. gentleman meets with concurrence on the part of his own associates.

I deny that in considering this Bill I have any associates except all the members of this House. I understand that this Bill is not introduced as a party measure, and I am expressing my own views irrespective of what others may think.

That is exactly what I am pointing out, namely, that it was the hon. gentleman's own view to disagree with me, and that in it he is not supported by those usually associated with him. I have often thought it strange that the hon. mem-

her for St. John cannot disagree with anything without denouncing it as absurd.
I do not think I used the word " absurd."
A reference to Hansard will be a wonderful revelation to my hon. friend.
I do not think I used the word.

If it is absurd to say that twenty-one years is a proper age for exercising the function of citizenship, and at the same time that eighteen is a proper age to enable a man to enlist as a soldier, then this absurdity has stood on the statute books of Canada all the time my hon. friend was minister, and all the time that his Government was in power. The Militia Act is there to say that a man may enlist at the age of eighteen.
A measure like this was never proposed before.
What has that to do with what I am discussing?
It has a great deal.

The hon. gbntleman said it was absurd to recognize twenty-one years as the age of full citizenship and eighteen years as the age of a soldier, and I say that principle had been recognized, and properly recognized, by his Government for fifteen years, and further, that it has been recognized by every Government in the civilized world.

During these fifteen
years, has the Solicitor General ever known that membership in the Canadian militia was considered sufficient to give a man the right to vote?
What has that to do with what I am discussing?
I would like to have an answer to my question.

Because the question never arose in these fifteen years; but can you describe as absurd the law of the United States, or the law of Great Britain, or the law of every civilized country, because it determines that a man may' be a soldier at eighteen years but may not reach the full maturity of citizenship until he is twenty-one years? What I argue is that the fact of a man's enlistment does not raise any presumption, that he is any more in a fit position to express more in-

telligently his views on public questions, ait the age of eighteen, than is his cousin of the same age at home. It is true that at the age of eighteen there are many soldiers as there are many civilians much more fit than those who have reached the age of forty to be entrusted with the franchise. But, you cannot base on the mere fact of his enlistment the presumption that he is fit to exercise the franchise at the age of eighteen. That is all I argued, and it does seem to me sound sense. At all events, that argument had the support of the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Graham) in very explicit language. I do not find any fault if one disagrees with me, but I do not think that the enunciation of so moderate a theory can be characterized as absurd. If a man enlists at the age of eighteen, the presumption is that he takes a more vital and patriotic interest in his country's affairs than if he had stayed at home, but the presumption does not arise that he is more developed mentally and Ithus more fitted to exercise the franchise than a person who has attained the age of twenty-one years. It does not seem fitting that the view which I have taken, and which is expressed in the legislation of many countries, should be lightly characterized as absurd.

I regret if I used the word "absurd," and if so I apologize. What I pointed out was that it was inconsistent for the Government to say that in respect to the votes of the soldiers, they will ignore all existing law, simply because the man is a soldier, except the law as to the age limit, and, when it comes to the age limit, that they will adhere rigidly to the existing law. The Solicitor General says that after all the question of importance is as to whether a man has arrived at the age when he may be reasonably expected to take an interest in his country's affairs, and what I argued was that a man of eighteen, who was patriotic enough and intelligent enough to volunteer for overseas service, having lived in Canada from the day of his birth may reasonably be presumed to have a better knowledge of the best interests of this country, and to be better able intelligently to cast his ballot, than the man who has had no home in Canada, who has not spent any part of his life in Canada, who may have come from any part of the world, and who, being a British subject, although an entire stranger to Canada, is given a vote simply because he has resided somewhere in Canada for the short period of thirty days before he enlisted. That is my

argument, and it seems to me it is impossible for any satisfactory answer to be given to it. If the Government insists upon conferring a new citizenship upon a great many men who are soldiers, they should extend it further, and they could, with the utmost safety, extend it to all those who do go to the front, whether they happen to be twenty-one or eighteen years of age.
Would my ho-n. friend extend the franchise to the bugler of fourteen?
Buglers do noi bear arms.
They are at the front.

I brought up the question; and, so far as I am concerned, the Solicitor General will understand that I want the vote given to all soldiers. If T have urged that the boy of eighteen should be given the right to vote, it is because he is just as well qualified as the boy of nineteen or twenty or twenty-one. Before the boy of eighteen can enlist, he is thoroughly inspected, mentally and physically; he is physically inspected from the top of his head to the bottom of his feet, and he must be found in every respect a fit subject for bearing arms and intelligent enough to comprehend and understand military movements of all kinds. If he is found physically or mentally unfit, he must stand aside, so that the young lad of eighteen who is competent to enlist is in every respect a perfect man who- is doing the same duty as the man who accidentally happens +o be a few months older than he is, and yet you are depriving him of the franchise simply because of an accident of birth.

It is recognized that the volunteer is so inspected and that he is passed on as physically within the requirements of the law and as mentally sound; but similarly a lad of five is just as mentally sound as a lad of eighteen, and in so far as military requirements are concerned, would on	that	score pass	the examination	justas	well	as would	the lad of eighteen.Therefore there would be just as much reason for admitting the youth of five to	the	franchise,	provided there	wassome capacity in which he could serve at	the	front, as	there would be	for
admitting the youth of eighteen. I do not like to be arguing against the extension of the franchise to any man who volunteers for such a great war as the one in which we are now engaged; but I do not
see any reason for presuming that because a man goes to the front, he is necessarily further advanced mentally and that he has a -more thorough knowledge and -a more competent power of expressing his interest in his country's affairs than the man who stays at home. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) says; What right have we to presume that because some one comes from the United States and lives in some part of Canada for thirty days, he has any interest in the affairs of Canada and should be given a vote? We have a right to presume it because he has come here to fight the battle of Canada.

The battle of the
Empire.

Any Britisher who has sufficient interest in the Empire-and -Canada is a part of the Empire-to come here to enlist as a soldier to fight the battle of the Empire in Europe is sufficiently interested in Canada to know how to vote.
Mr. OLIVER; The hon. gentleman does not give him the right to vote unless he is a British subject.
Certainly not. Does the hon. gentleman argue that we should give it to those who are not British subjects?

The hon. gentleman has
argued that himself.

I am not arguing that. Naturally a subject of His Majesty who comes here from the United States or anywhere else who wishes to serve the country to which he belongs and who is willing to expose his life in that service, demonstrates that he has sufficient interest in the affairs of this country to entitle him to vote.

But you will not give
the vote to a youth of nineteen who has lived in Canada all his life?

Not because he has not sufficient interest-I made that very clear when I spoke first; he has sufficient interest and he has demonstrated that in the most convincing way that any man could demonstrate it-but because he has not reached the age when by the laws of our country he is competent to express that interest. If we could presume that merely because he enlisted he was further advanced than he would otherwise be in his mental competence, then we would give him the right to vote.

In the case of a civilian, the law requires a residence, we shall say, of a year. Do you not presume that a man, because he goes to the front, has
5 p.m. a more active and deeper interest in the welfare of his country than the civilian has? You allow him to vote simply on a short term residence of thirty days.

That man by goi.ng to
the front demonstrates that he has that interest which is at the bottom of our franchise.
What more interest has he in the welfare of Canada than the man who stays at home and does his duty at home by the soldiers at the front?

Now we are on another point. There may be many at home who are not doing their duty at all; but if we extended the franchise and made it universal applicable to wanderers with no local habitaltion, they all would also have the right to vote. We have no right to presume that merely because a man stays in Canada he has that interest in his country's affairs which is at the bottom of the franchise; but we have a right to presume that because a man goes to the war, he has that interest. I do not think I could express my own mind better if I spoke longer.
Hear, hear.
Nor what is in the mind of the right hon. leader of the Opposition.

If a citizen of the United States of America comes across the boundary line and enlists in the army of the Empire through Canada and takes the risks of war, inasmuch as he has rendered all the service to this country that he can render; that he is making the supreme sacrifice that any man can make, and that he is making it for Canada and for the Empire, why should that man not be recognized as having a reasonable and sufficient interest in Canada to allow him to vote? If any man is to be recognized as having done any special service to the country entitling him to special recognition because of his enlistment, I say: Why is not every man entitled to that same recognition?

I will answer my hon. friend in this way. The fact that an American citizen comes to Canada and enlists for the war goes to show that he has some

interest in Canada and the Empire. The question is: does it go far enough? The hon. member for Edmonton will agree with me that a British subject should have higher rights to citizenship in Canada than an alien, and that the fact that a man is an alien creates the presumption against him and makes the usual adverse presumption founded on non-residence here much more difficult to be overcome. The fact, that a British subject resides in the United States raises the presumption against him that he has not an interest in Canada's-affairs unless he overcomes that presumption by some act. If he comes here and volunteers for the front, then we say it is overcome; but if he is an alien, if he is not only a resident of the United States, but a citizen of that country, then the fact that he volunteers is not to my mind sufficient to overcome the presumption.

Take a Sikh from India or the other immigrants from India who have been coming into British Columbia. My hon. friend would propose to give them the right to cast their ballot simply because they happened to arrive thirty days before enlisting, although the young man of eighteen or nineteen or twenty, who as I said has lived all his life in Canada, knows a thousand times more about the real interests of Canada and the issues dividing the parties than a stranger could possibly know, be cause no man coming into this country and residing simply for thirty days can become seized of the issues which affect the two parties unless he has" an intellect far and away beyond that of the ordinary citizen. Surely my hon. friend must see that, either we ought not to extend the franchise at all, or if we recognize that the fact that, a soldier goes to the war is a reason for extending his right of citizenship, we ought to give the same right to the young man between eighteen and twenty-one who goes to the front and risks his life just the same as any other soldier does.
If we extend the franchise to those who enlist for service abroad, we should also extend it to the young men of Canada who have lived in this country all their lives, whose hearts are with Canada and who are in a position to vote more intelligently than strangers who have been in this country only for a short period of thirty days.

I have repeatedly given
the reasons why I object to this provision, and I desire now to move to strike out
the proviso of section 1.

Aside from the Niobe, the Rainbow and the submarines, there are other steamers and vessels belonging to the Government upon which are serving a large number of persons who are qualified to vote in the maritime constituencies of Can

ada. They have always found it difficult to register their votes at the time of a general election. I do not see why it should not be possible for these boats to be in the harbour of Esquimalt, Vancouver, or some other port, so that the men serving on them would not be completely debarred from casting their votes. There must be 50 boats in the naval service, the crews of which lose their votes at every election. Is no provision being made for them?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The provision which
the hon. member desires is not peculiar to the present situation. No doubt we may sometime devise provisions whereby absentees may vote; the experience of other countries which have adopted such legislation indicates that it is not an impossibility. So far as the naval force is concerned, the number of men serving on the different vessels who would otherwise be voters is not very large, while the soldiers are people who would have been entitled to vote if they had been at home.

It is provided here that when a soldier comes to register his vote, the official who receives it must decide whether the soldier has a right to vote anywhere else. I cannot see that any machinery is provided by which that difficulty is to be settled.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Precisely the machin-
' ery that is provided when that situation arises before a deputy returning officer and where the man is sworn.

There is this difference:
when the voter comes before the deputy returning officer and is sworn, witnesses and other persons are present, the act is a public act which renders the man liable within the knowledge of those who represent either one candidate or the other. There is a restriction there, in the public interest; under this legislation there is no such restriction, and there is no possibility of there being any. My hon. friend may say: you are unjustly imputing impropriety of some kind. I say we are not imputing any more impropriety than we are when we enforce the provisions of the Elections Act. The vote counts just the same, whether it is cast
under the very loose conditions provided by this Bill, or under the conditions provided by the Elections Act. We are dealing with something in which is involved the control of the affairs of Canada, and I think that when the Government comes forward with a measure that undertakes to introduce an entirely new principle and an entirely new method of procedure, we are entitled to say that we require adequate safeguards, of the same purport and effect as those cast around similar proceedings under the Elections Act. This proposed legislation absolutely fails in that regard, and in order to relieve the situation as much as possible, I want to reduce the possibility of varying the conditions unfairly or unjustly. That is why I move that this proviso be struck out. The amendment which the hon. minister has made with regard to the qualification of thirty days' residence provides that every man who is entitled to vote shall vote; it gives him the right to express his view. When you have done that, you have done what you can for the soldiers; now I ask you to do what you can for the body politic by ensuring that there shall not be any switching of ballots. This is an unpleasant subject to deal with, and I do not intend to go into the details. I have already pointed out to the hon. minister the conditions which prevail at Edmonton, Calgary and many other places, and if this provision remains in the Bill, there is an opportunity to switch the ballots where they will do the most good. My hon. friend knows that that is not desirable and proper; I assume that it is not his intention that it shall happen, but the provisions of the Bill make it entirely possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The remedy the hon. gentleman offers seems to me to be intended to prevent the possibility of switching any ballots by providing by law to switch all the ballots. I think, looking at it from the standpoint of the interest of the body politic, that interest is that we should do everything we can do to keep these votes in the district to which they would naturally belong. The remedy the hon. gentleman suggests is to take them all, holus bolus, out of that district.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot agree with him that that would be the best way to remedy the difficulty. As to the discussion about precautions, we can best deal with that when we come to the section which deals with the method of voting.

I wish to take exception to the comparison made by the minister that -instead of part of the ballots being switched all should be switched. There is no such proposal as to switch all the ballots by striking out this proviso. A large proportion of voters were resident in the districts in which they were entitled to vote for 30 days before their enlistment. While, theoretically or on the face of it, the hon. minister might be warranted in using the expression he did, as a matter of actual practice there is no sufficient warrant for his sweeping statement. I maintain that while there might be some restriction of the right of the voter to vote in the district in which he was entitled to vote originally, that would be very limited under the very desirable provision that he has made in regard to 30 days' residence. I think that the amendment which he proposes has relieved the situation so that this proviso, even from his own point of view, is not really necessary or advantageous.

The minister states that the difficulty I pointed out as arising from that proviso is met easily and effectively by some affidavit that can be prepared of the voter. I can find only one affidavit here dealing with that. With regard to putting safeguards around the vote, we might as well try to put safeguards around the rays of the moon and keep it from shining on the earth as to put safeguards around this poll. We have to be very careful that we do not use any strong language. The word "absurd," for instance, is prohibited and some other adjectives; but I venture to say there are no adjectives known to Worcester, Webster or Walker that would do anything like justice-
Mr. DuHERTY: I suggest that the hon. member try the Century dictionary.
There is not much new in Webster, Worcester or Walker, and if it will please my hon. friend I will add the Century to Webster, Worcester and Walker.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You ought to try it first.

And I may say to my hon. friend and to the hon. member for Calgary who have fathered this thing, that it is a thing of beauty in itself which both of them could fall down and worship without any fear of being guilty of any idolatry, for it is not like anything in the heavens

above nor on the earth beneath nor in the waters under the earth. The minister said yesterday that the affidavit was copied. Well, perhaps it was. I believe the minister when he said the Bill was not copied. I can readily understand that, because they certainly could not find anything like this to copy. It is a most serious thing for us to conceive that some 25,000 or 30,000, perhaps 50,000 men, of the most heterogeneous character of people that could be conceived of, and under the most adverse circumstances to obtain order or regularity, shall be let loose on polling day. They will be all scrambling for some position where they can poll their votes. There will be nobody there who will know them, nobody who can keep the slightest check as to who they are. As a rule, in towns and particularly rural districts, the presiding officer at the poll is well known and knows everybody in the district; and the presence of a respectable man sitting at the poll box is to some extent security for those who are interested in the election to see that the right thing is done. But here we are in the forests of northern France or somewhere with these men casting their votes before a stranger who knows nothing about them or where they should vote. One man could come in 30 times and vote if he was bad enough to do so. These men will be no better there than at home, and they would do it at home. The minister knows that there is personation by the hundred thousand in elections. If he does not, I tell him it is done. I tell him it was done in my county a year ago last February by his party, done over and over again; and now we are told upon the faith of the goodness of the people, because they crossed the Atlantic they lose all their sin and iniquities, they are washed away in the Atlantic, and these men are now so pure, honest and good that we offend the minister by suggesting that some safeguard should be thrown around this poll. He tells me there is an affidavit here that will prevent them from representing themselves as voting in one place whereas in truth they belong to another. I cannot find it. I think I should ask if there is such a proviso, and in doing so I to some extent relieve my own responsibility by giving another slight conception to the minister of my aversion to this Bill from stem to stern, and to everything about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The observations of the hon. gentleman will come in better when we come to deal with the methods and precautions provided. I want to assure him,

for the moment, that if I had had any conception that I was. providing for votes for " hydrogeneous " people, I certainly would never have introduced this legislation. When we come to deal with this matter I shall certainly see that anything that gives votes to hydrogeneous people is eliminated.
Amendment of Mr. Oliver negatived; amendment of Mr. Doherty agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 2-distribution of ballot papers:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Bill originally provided for the sending of ballots not only to the commanding officer in Bermuda and to the secretary of the High Commissioner in England, but likewise to the officers commanding the forces at military posts in Canada. It is proposed by the amendments that will come in their proper order to provide that all soldiers in Canada shall vote on the ordinary election day in the ordinary and usual way, with this exception simply, that the ballot shall be provided for them at the places where they are and that they shall be allowed to so vote outside of the electoral districts in which they are to vote. I therefore propose to amend this section by striking out all reference to commanding officers at the bases and camps in Canada, and it will then read as follows:
2. A sufficient supply of ballot papers in form A of this Act and of envelopes for holding the same with affidavits in form B printed thereon shall be sent by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to the officer in command of the Canadian troops at Bermuda and to the secretary of the High Commissioner for Canada in London, England, and such papers and envelopes shall be kept by such officer in command and the secretary of the High Commissioner.

As I read the section, no date is set when it becomes the duty of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to send out these ballots. Is it the intention that he shall send them out as soon as the Bill becomes law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It might be so. I had not in mind the necessity of fixing any particular time for doing that. The idea of this Bill is to create a situation where, if an election did come on, things would be in such shape that it would be possible for the soldiers to exercise their votes. Under the Bill it is proposed that these ballots shall be in the possession of the secretary to the High Commissioner, and of the officer at Bermuda, for use should occasion require. I would understand the Bill to mean that the ballots will be sent whether or not any one concerned contemplates an election in the near future.
There is a period of five or six weeks between the issuing of the writ and polling day. It seems to me that is quite sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the thing is to be -effective at all it is very important to do what can be done to make sure that the ballots get back in time. As regards Bermuda, it might be possible to send out the ballots and get them back within the five or six weeks; but it is difficult for us to calculate just how long it would take to send them across the ocean to the secretary of the High Commissioner, and then across the Channel, and into France, and so on. What we can do to reduce to a minimum the risk oif those ballots not being back in time, I think we ought to do. I cannot see that any evil is likely to result from putting a certain number of blank ballots in the hands of persons designated in this section. It simply puts us that much more forward at the time of the election writ. The ballots would remain in London. Another section provides that upon communication with the secretary of the High Commissioner, the machinery for getting these ballots to the proper officers can at once be set going. It is of course uncertain how long it may take to get the ballots to the soldiers and back here again. This provision was made simply because it was thought that there were advantages in avoiding delays so far as we could, and that no harm could come from having a certain number of blank ballots entrusted to the secretary of the High Commissioner.

Should not this section be considered in connection with the suggestion which the right hon. leader of the Opposition has made, and which the minister said he would take into consideration. I doubt very much whether it will inspire public confidence to have a large number of printed ballots sent to the office of the High Commissioner, who is a member of the Government. We know how carefully ballots have always to be preserved, because one of the things which might be done by persons who took an interest in political matters, would be to have the ballots switched. There is no safeguard for keeping the marked ballot attached to the affidavit. That could be changed by a person desiring to do it. And, therefore, if there are to be commissioners, it seems to me the ballots ought to be placed in the custody of the two commissioners and kept in a place of safety.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, these ballots have no value in themselves until they are marked. While the office of the High Commissioner is mentioned in the Bill, a modification has been made to provide that they shall go to the secretary of the High Commissioner, and shall be kept by him. We were endeavouring to select a permanent official. After all we are trusting the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to have these ballots in his possession. Is there any more danger in entrusting them to the secretary of the High Commissioner?

Except that he is a
servant of the Parliament of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I think the secretary of the High Commissioner is the servant of the people of Canada.
The servant of the High Commissioner.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course, the High
Commissioner is the chief officer, but I do not understand that he appoints or dismisses the secretary at his will. So far, the secretary has certainly been treated as a permanent official. I suppose I am lacking in the capacity that enables one to see so far into a milestone as some people can, and to be quite as suspicious as it may be quite justifiable to be. But frankly, I am at a loss to know why it is more dangerous to have these blank ballots in the hands of the secretary to the High Commissioner than it is to have them in the hands of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery described as the secretary of Parliament as distinguished from the secretary to the High Commissioner, who is the servant of the people of Canada. But if anybody is afraid, and if I can work it out so that I shall not be depriving the soldier of his vote because of the delay in sending over these ballots until the last minute, I shall be glad to join in the distrust of the secretary. But, to be perfectly frank, I do not grasp why it is objectionable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

And I suppose you would have to take the ordinary precautions. I do not see there is any provision in this Bill for a special count to be made of the ballots. The Clerk of the Crown in Chancery has to answer for what he does and whenever he sends ballots out of his office he keeps a record of how ' many have been taken and the party to whom the ballots are issued has also to give an account of the number that he has received, the number that he has used and the number that he has returned. These precautions are enjoined upon those who have to do with the voting in an ordinary election and it seems to me that similar precautions ought to be required in this Bill.

I have noticed that in the New Zealand Bill they seem to have thought it necessary to take some precaution in regard to the ballots because they provide that the electoral officer shall issue ballots only to those who make application for them. This Bill provides that whether the soldier is given a vote or not the ballot is to be distributed and it may be that these ballots may get into the hands of those for whom they were not intended.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
While I cannot claim to have foreseen everything in the drafting of this Bill, I can olaim to have learned something from some of the observations which have been made. There would be some advantage if hon. members would let us get to the sections that deal with the matters in regard to which they have apprehensions so that I could explain them and we could make some progress. Hon. gentlemen are perfectly justified in criti-

cising the Bill as it is before them and in the form in which it was presented, but if that criticism were made when we came to the sections dealing with these particular subjects, I would be able to p-int out that we have improved upon the rsill as originally presented by providing that the ballot shall only be handed by the officer to such volunteers as take the affidavit. I must say that in thinking the matter over myself it did strike me tnat a very dangerous situation might result from distributing ballots around and I therefore propose to provide an amendment that shall require tnat a soldier, in order to receive the ballot, must first take the affidavit.

Does not the minister
think I ought to be forgiven when I take the Bill as we have it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
1 not only think you
ought to be forgiven out I assure you you are forgiven.

The Bill has been all
torn to pieces by the minister. He comes to-day with a new Bill which has not even been typewritten, which is not printed; none of us knows what it is, we are groping in the dark, and the minister is unfolding to us this wonderful production which none of us has had an opportunity of seeing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think there is -some force in what the hon. gentleman says about the printing of the proposed amendments, which, as I understand, are very important.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, they are.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
So, I think that at six o'clock we will rise and proceed with some other business.
Mr.*DOHERTY: I think I perhaps owe some apology to-hon. gentlemen for the fact that the Bill is not printed. I can understand that some inconvenience may be occasioned by it, but we would have avoided some of that inconvenience if there had been a greater readiness to deal with the Bill section by section. I admit that the Bill has called for a great deal of amendment. I am quite willing to admit even that some of the tearing to pieces of the Bill, which the hon. gentleman attributes to me, was contributed to by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, and perhaps I ought to thank them for it. I announced at the beginning that I was willing to learn, and I am not ashamed to say that I have learned very many things.
I suppose my hon. friend will not bo offended if I say that I have learned some things from them, and I am trying'to put these things into operation. I would have been glad if time had made it possible for the Bill to be reprinted. I did ask to have a certain number of typewritten copies.
If there were some typewritten copies it would be an assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I trust my hon. friends will forgive me for this.
I will forgive you.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In view of such kindly forgiveness, might I suggest that this second section be allowed to pass?
Hear, hear.
I am sure I am satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If you can find a method by which these ballots can be improved later on, we certainly will be glad to consider it.
I hope ihe right hon. the Prime Minister will not in future say that this House unanimously agreed to the section because we allow it to be carried.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If you allow it to carry unanimously, I shall certainly not.
Some other inscription should be put on the ballot-something designating that it is for a Dominion general election or that it is for a soldier's vote.

I understand from the right hon. Prime Minister that we may rise and finish the Bill later, because clauses 3 and 4 are what I might call the iniquitous clauses of this Bill. The Minister of Justice has 'had two days on this Bill now, and he is only beginning to see light through it. I am afraid that before ihe gets through at all many days will have elapsed. I would suggest to the minister that he had better abandon it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If it is going to take so long in the future there is all the more reason for utilizing the twenty minutes before six o'clock.

There are two things I mentioned yesterday I hat I want again to draw to the attention of the minister. I refer, first, to a member of the paymaster's staff or an officer who is himself a candidate having to do with the taking of tbi* vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have a clause providing for that.

The next matter to which I want to draw the minister's attention has reference to taking the votes of the soldiers in Canada. I want to urge upon him the necessity of providing all the .safeguards that we have in an ordinary election when taking this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the clause I have in my mind will carry out the two suggestions which the hon. gentleman made yesterday. I propose to provide that no officer who is a candidate shall act in any capacity in carrying out this Act. Another provision in regard to the soldiers at home is that they shall vote under the same conditions as the ordinary voter votes with this exception that we will provide returning officers and polling places at the camps where the men can vote and register their votes although these votes will be applicable in other districts. In substance, the entire procedure provided for by the Dominion Elections Act is followed except in two things. For instance, the returning officer will not have to hold a nomination and he will have to take some means of ascertaining who the volunteers in the camp are who claim the right to vote, where they claim the right to vote and so "forth. But in so far as the method is concerned, when it comes to the actual voting, we provide that the deputy returning officer shall proceed as in an ordinary election and on the ordinary election day. When it comes to actual voting we propose to provide a deputy returning officer who would take that vote as nearly as possible as it is taken in ordinary elections, and to take it on the ordinary election day.

It will be taken on
election day ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Taken on election day.

It has been represented
to me that the censorship which is over all communications from the trenches might interfere with the secrecy of the ballot. The ballot is supposed to be absolutely secret and a man might write anything he likes upon it and some persons have represented to me that it will be liable to interfere with the strict censorship that is on everything that comes from the trenches.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is possible that if
the censors thought there were any occasion to censor correspondence addressed to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery they

might open the ballots, and censor them, but that is rather a remote possibility, if it be a possibility at all. Of course, if necessary, the censorship authorities might be communicated with, and I fancy they would not be adverse to letting the ballots come to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery.
It would not do to let the censors open the packages, because the secrecy of the ballot would be destroyed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If these ballots, when
they arrive, indicate that they have been opened they will not be counted.
As I understand it, there will be only one day set for taking the vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Do you mean in Canada?
No, in the trenches.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We do not propose to take these votes on election day. The ballots will be sent to the officers who will issue them and take the affidavits and receive the votes and mail them back, but there is no provision that that should be done on one day, or as to when it should be done. If these ballots get back to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery in time to be forwarded to the returning officer of the different electoral districts by polling day they will be counted; otherwise they will not.

The return of the candi-
*date will not be delayed by waiting for the ballots?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is not proposed.

Suppose certain ballots should come to the returning officer in a riding, and the returning officer and the candidates and everybody knows that the votes sent there do not lawfully belong to that electoral district, and the proofs are positive as to that, what would happen?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The remedies in that case would be just the same for the soldier vote as they are with regard to the votes polled at any election which are polled as a consequence of a false oath. I have no doubt that, under such circumstances, upon a protest, the votes would be struck out.
But if that offence were committed in this country, the man could be prosecuted for perjury?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To be perfectly frank, I do not contend that we could convict a man in this country for having committed! perjury in France or Belgium.
And therefore you provide a penalty that you cannot enforce.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The penalties may not reach everybody, but they are provided for offences,, which I think the right hon. gentleman will find are quite susceptible of being committed in Canada.
And out of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And out of Canada. The law will reach anybody within the limits of Canada, so that the penalties provided are not wholly nugatory. I do not think we would be justified in leaving out these penalties because they do not extend so far as we would like them to.
If an offence in connection with this Act should be committed by a soldier in Canada, could the legal punishment be applied to him?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I know of no reason why the punishment is not susceptible of being applied to a soldier. There may be conditions prevailing in this country which might justify the military authorities resisting any attempt of the civil power to proceed against a soldier, but as an abstract proposition, when a man becomes a soldier he becomes bound by the military law, but he does not cease to be bound by the civil law.

As far as an abstract
